Abstract Ambient ammonia synthesis is important for carbon neutrality. Tribo-electro-catalysis, which converts mechanical friction into chemical driving force through contact electrification and charge transfer, offers a route for nitrogen (N2) fixation. However, inefficient utilization of friction-induced charges and insufficient N2 activation remain major challenges. Herein, acid-etching defect engineering regulates the surface and electronic structures of lead telluride (PbTe) for N2 fixation. The catalyst etched for 90 min exhibits the enhanced activity under dark ambient conditions, delivering ammonium (NH4+) production rates of 258.98 and 329.60 μmol L–1·g–1·h–1 without and with 10 vol % methanol, respectively. Analyses reveal that etching reconstructs the surface, generates defect sites, facilitates N2 adsorption and activation, and promotes friction-induced charge utilization. Excessive etching decreases activity. Charge-trapping and electron paramagnetic resonance measurements support the role of friction-induced negative charges, establishing defect-mediated charge regulation as an effective strategy for sustainable ammonia synthesis.

Additive Manufacturing (AM) of electrical machine windings has highlighted new design opportunities for increasing system power density, but applying a robust electrical insulation coating to coils that are manufactured in an as-wound but uninsulated state is challenging. The localised surface heating generated in induction heating offers an attractive method for processing high-performance insulation on such complex prefabricated geometry as it directly heats the insulation-metal boundary. This paper investigates whether the temperature response from heating with a standard solenoid driving coil is suitable for the processing of Poly-Ether-Ether-Ketone (PEEK), both analytically and experimentally. The analytical model predicts the maximum temperature found empirically within 2%, suggesting predictability in this process. Furthermore, the heating is consistent between trials with a maximum observed difference of 4.6%. However, the current arrangement produces a temperature non-uniformity with a range of 147 °C, which would result in the thermal degradation of PEEK, and changes to the process are considered in order to successfully process PEEK on AM electrical machine windings.
